I am sixty-seven years old, and I have farmed these flat lands of Quzhou County since I was a young girl. I only finished primary school, but the land has been my teacher for over fifty years. My children have gone to work in the cities, so it is just my husband and me now. We have about five mu of good land, and I know every corner of it. I do not try anything fancy. Everyone around here grows wheat and maize in rotation, and that is what I will do this year too.

My wheat went in last October before the frost. Now it is spring, and the wheat is turning green. I will give it the first spring irrigation soon, and spread the topdressing fertilizer — I buy compound fertilizer from the township supply shop, the kind the village extension agent recommends. I will water three or four times before we harvest in early June. We should get about five hundred kilograms per mu if the weather cooperates. I also watch for pests and spray when I see aphids or rust; usually that means two insecticide sprays, one herbicide, and one fungicide.

After we cut the wheat in early June, I will plant maize right away. I do not plow again — I just drill the hybrid maize seed into the wheat stubble. I buy the seed from the shop, usually a Denghai variety. Maize does not need as much water as wheat; two irrigations in the summer are enough. I spray for pests three or four times. I expect about five hundred and fifty kilograms per mu from the maize. I thought about planting cotton on a small patch, but at my age I do not have the back for all that hand-picking and spraying. Wheat and maize are easier — the combine comes to the village, and the grain buyers pay cash at the door. That is my plan.
